whyCorrect: "Far from being a _____ record" signals that the blank names the quality the sketchbook lacks, and the evidence after the comma is revisions, abandoned starts and figures redrawn several times. What that evidence rules out is the idea that the sketchbook straightforwardly reproduces what the painter saw. A faithful record is one that reproduces its subject accurately, so it is exactly the description the sentence denies.

whyWrong.B: Revisions and repeated redrawing suggest slow, laboured work, so "hurried" is what the sketchbook arguably is, not what the sentence denies it is.
whyWrong.C: Pages full of revisions and multiple attempts are not less detailed than a clean copy; the contrast in the sentence is about accuracy to the subject, not about the amount of detail.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the sentence concerns who was meant to see the sketchbook, and a book of private working drawings would fit the evidence rather than contradict it.

tips: When a sentence opens with "Far from being a _____," the blank must be the opposite of the evidence that follows.

whyCorrect: The blank is defined by the clause that follows it: the novel doubles back on events already shown and retells them from a second vantage point. You need a word for a structure that returns to and repeats its own earlier material. "Recursive" names exactly that self-returning pattern.

whyWrong.A: "Conventional" describes how ordinary a structure is, not what it does; a structure that repeatedly doubles back is in fact unusual.
whyWrong.B: Linear is the opposite of what the sentence describes — a linear novel moves forward through events once, never revisiting them.
whyWrong.D: "Abrupt" describes sudden transitions, which is a matter of pace; the sentence describes the novel returning to earlier events, not moving suddenly.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts confining herself to one medium with working in three, and "with equal _____, moving between them throughout her career" describes how she handled all three. The blank needs a quality she possessed in each medium alike, and the point of the contrast is that no medium restricted her. "Facility" means ease or skill, so working in all three with equal facility says she was equally at home in each.

whyWrong.A: "Obscurity" describes how little known something is, which says nothing about her handling of the materials and contradicts a sentence praising her range.
whyWrong.B: "Restraint" would describe her holding back in each medium, which does not follow from a sentence about moving freely among them.
whyWrong.C: "Reluctance" makes the sentence say she was equally unwilling to use all three media, contradicting the fact that she used them throughout her career.

whyCorrect: "Although" sets up a contrast: the technique was built for one material, frescoes, and something surprising was found about a second material, textiles. The word "also" tells you the technique works on textiles too. "Applicable to textiles" says the technique can be used on them, which is the surprise the contrast requires.

whyWrong.B: "Comparable to textiles" would compare the technique itself with textiles, which is not a sensible comparison and does not say the technique can be used on them.
whyWrong.C: "Preferable" needs something to be preferred over; the sentence offers no competing method, and it would not explain the "as well."
whyWrong.D: "Susceptible" describes something vulnerable to harm, which reverses the relationship — the technique is used on textiles, not damaged by them.

whyCorrect: The colon means the second half of the sentence defines the blank, and it reports an even split: three papers endorse the theory and three reject it. That is a live disagreement among specialists. "Contested" is the word for a claim that specialists are actively arguing over.

whyWrong.A: "Obscure" would mean the theory is little known, but six recent papers discussing it show that specialists know it well.
whyWrong.B: "Outdated" would mean specialists have moved past it, which the three endorsements contradict.
whyWrong.C: "Settled" is the reverse of the evidence — a settled theory is one specialists agree on, and here they are evenly divided.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences explain a cause: glass cools too fast to crystallise, so its molecules stay disordered. The underlined sentence opens with "This is why," which marks it as an effect of that explanation, and it reports something you can observe when handling glass — no grain, cuttable in any direction. That is a practical consequence drawn from the account of glass's structure.

whyWrong.A: No term is defined here; "grain" is introduced in the underlined sentence rather than being an earlier term explained by it.
whyWrong.B: The sentence closes the point rather than opening one, and the text develops no distinction after it.
whyWrong.D: It follows logically from the preceding claim rather than contradicting it — disordered molecules are precisely why there is no grain.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the underlined one sets up Ayrton's appearance before the Institution; the sentence after it reports that she traced the hissing to a chemical reaction and eliminated it. The underlined sentence sits between them and describes the hissing as a nuisance that had defeated better-funded laboratories for years. That detail exists to show the problem was hard and worth solving, which makes her solution matter.

whyWrong.B: The sentence mentions the better-funded laboratories only to say they failed; it says nothing about how their methods differed from hers.
whyWrong.C: The text never links the paper's subject to the invitation, and the underlined sentence gives no reason she was asked to speak.
whyWrong.D: It concedes nothing about Ayrton's own work; the limitation described belongs to the other laboratories.

whyCorrect: The text says seawater percolating through the material reacts with volcanic ash to grow interlocking crystals in the cracks, and then that the concrete is strengthened by the same process that destroys modern concrete. So the durability comes from cracks being filled by crystals that the seawater itself helps produce.

whyWrong.A: The text says seawater percolates into the material and reacts with the ash; the ash draws seawater in rather than repelling it.
whyWrong.B: Water content of the mix is never mentioned; the water that matters in the passage is seawater entering afterward.
whyWrong.D: The passage assumes the concrete does crack — the crystals grow in the cracks — so a mix that resists cracking altogether is the opposite of the mechanism described.

whyCorrect: The text describes the solutions in one sentence: they "never settled and never repeated." That is the notable property, and it is why they were later recognised as early examples of chaos. Option A restates both halves of that description.

whyWrong.B: The text says nothing about how the solutions were computed, and Cartwright worked in the 1930s, before electronic computers.
whyWrong.C: The text says the solutions were later recognised in a general theory of chaos, which means they extended beyond radio amplifiers.
whyWrong.D: This contradicts the text directly — the solutions never repeated, whether after a delay or otherwise.

whyCorrect: The conclusion rests entirely on the assumption that the isolated males heard no adult song, so anything they still produce must be innate. If those males could hear recordings of adult song elsewhere in the facility, the isolation was incomplete and the opening phrase could have been learned like the rest. That removes the only support for calling it innate.

whyWrong.B: A shorter opening phrase still means isolated males produce the phrase without a model, which is consistent with it being innate rather than damaging to the claim.
whyWrong.C: How often the birds sing has no bearing on whether the content of the song was learned or inherited.
whyWrong.D: Variation among wild males concerns the learned portion of the song and leaves the claim about the innate opening phrase untouched.

commonMistakes: Weakening a claim means attacking the evidence it depends on; here that evidence is the birds' isolation, not the song's length.

whyCorrect: The linguist has to separate two candidate causes that occurred together: schooling policy and migration to cities. The strongest support is a case where one varies and the other does not. Neighbouring communities with the same migration rates but bilingual schooling kept their language, which isolates schooling as the factor that made the difference.

whyWrong.A: Steady migration shows migration did not spike alongside the shift, which is helpful but only removes one rival; it never shows schooling did anything.
whyWrong.B: Elders still speaking the language describes how far the shift went, not what caused it.
whyWrong.D: When the policy ended says nothing about whether it caused the shift while it was in force.

tips: To support a claim that A rather than B caused an outcome, look for a comparison case where B is held constant and A changes.

whyCorrect: The engineer is choosing between two causes, pedestrians and wind, so the useful finding is one that separates them. Swaying that occurred on days with little or no wind rules wind out, and its occurring specifically whenever the bridge was crowded ties the motion to the pedestrians. That is both halves of the engineer's argument in one observation.

whyWrong.B: Design capacity shows the bridge should survive strong wind, not that wind failed to move it; the swaying could still be wind-driven and harmless.
whyWrong.C: Feeling unsteady is an effect of the swaying, so it happens whatever the cause and distinguishes nothing.
whyWrong.D: A closed bridge has neither pedestrians nor, necessarily, the same exposure to wind; with both removed, the observation cannot point to either cause.

whyCorrect: The final sentence sets a condition: suppose bold foxes are the ones that move in near roads to begin with. Then the difference the study measured was already present before any fox experienced traffic, and the correlation reflects self-selection rather than an effect of roads. So the finding may only show where bold foxes settle.

whyWrong.A: Adding juveniles addresses the researchers' separate caution about sampling only adults; it does not answer the self-selection problem the last sentence raises, and it would test the finding rather than strengthen it.
whyWrong.C: The concern raised is about what causes the difference, not about which locations the result generalises to.
whyWrong.D: This is the causal claim the sentence has just given you a reason to doubt, so it is the conclusion the condition blocks.

commonMistakes: An "if" clause at the end of an inference text is usually a rival explanation; the completion should follow from it, not restate the original claim.

whyCorrect: The scholarly assumption was that Corbie invented the letterform. The new evidence is a securely dated charter from three hundred kilometres away using the same form forty years earlier, which means the form existed before Corbie used it. The minimum conclusion that follows is that the Corbie scribes took up a letterform already in use elsewhere.

whyWrong.B: Where the Corbie scribes trained is a specific route of transmission the text gives no evidence for; earlier use elsewhere does not establish who taught whom.
whyWrong.C: Independent invention would leave the earlier charter unexplained as a source and is exactly the possibility the new date makes unnecessary to assume.
whyWrong.D: Copying a single charter into their manuscripts is a much stronger claim than sharing a letterform, and the text describes only the letterform in common.

whyCorrect: "Because the samples had been stored improperly" begins with a subordinating conjunction, so it is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone. A dependent clause placed in front of a main clause is joined to it with a comma, giving "Because the samples had been stored improperly, the team could not use them."

whyWrong.A: "And" joins two elements of equal rank, but the first half is dependent because of "Because," so the sentence never reaches a main clause.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, and the "Because" clause is not independent.
whyWrong.D: A colon also requires a complete independent clause before it, which "Because the samples had been stored improperly" is not.

commonMistakes: Seeing two long word groups and assuming both are sentences; check the first word — "because," "although," "when" and "since" all make the clause dependent.

whyCorrect: "Each of which helps date the layers around it" contains the relative pronoun "which," so it is a relative clause that has to stay attached to the noun it describes rather than becoming its own sentence. A comma is the punctuation that attaches a non-restrictive relative clause to the main clause.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and a "which" clause cannot stand alone, so this leaves a fragment after the semicolon.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or list; a relative clause beginning with "each of which" is neither, and it still needs to be joined to its noun.
whyWrong.D: A period creates a fragment after it, and the lowercase "each" shows the clause was never built to start a sentence.

whyCorrect: "Marie Tharp spent years plotting soundings by hand" and "the result was the first map to show the mid-Atlantic ridge as a continuous feature" are both complete sentences. Two independent clauses joined with no conjunction need a semicolon.

whyWrong.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all the two clauses run together as a fused sentence.
whyWrong.D: A colon already does the joining, so adding "and" doubles the connector; the pair is not a legal combination.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: the design reduced material use, and it cut assembly time. To join two independent clauses you need either a semicolon or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, and "a fifth, and it also cut" supplies the second of those.

whyWrong.A: A comma with no conjunction between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: The semicolon itself is legal, but "also it also cut" states "also" twice, which is not idiomatic English.
whyWrong.C: With nothing between the clauses the sentence is fused.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is "Each," not "prototypes" — "of the three prototypes" is a prepositional phrase, and a subject never sits inside one. "Each" is singular, so it takes the singular verb "has."

whyWrong.A: "Were having" is plural and also puts a state of possession into the progressive, which English does not do with "have" meaning "possess."
whyWrong.B: "Have" is the plural form, agreeing with "prototypes" instead of with the real subject "Each."
whyWrong.D: "Having" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb at all.

tips: Cross out any "of …" phrase before choosing the verb; what is left is the true subject.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between the results in this trial and the results in the earlier trial, so the pronoun stands in for the plural noun "results." "Those" is the plural demonstrative that can take a modifier after it, giving "more consistent than those obtained in the earlier trial."

whyWrong.A: "That" is singular and cannot stand for the plural "results."
whyWrong.C: "Them" is an object pronoun and cannot be modified by the participial phrase "obtained in the earlier trial" in this comparative structure.
whyWrong.D: "It" is singular and also refers to a thing rather than to a plural set of results.

whyCorrect: The "not only … but also" pair has to link matching forms, and the first half uses the past tense "did … damage." The second half needs a past-tense finite verb of its own, so "it also breached the harbour wall" completes the parallel.

whyWrong.A: "Breach" is the bare present form and does not agree with the singular subject "it" or match the past tense of the first half.
whyWrong.B: "Had breach" is not a verb form; the perfect requires the participle "breached."
whyWrong.C: "Breaching" is a participle with no auxiliary, so the second clause is left without a finite verb.

whyCorrect: The first sentence leaves you expecting a problem: lead pipes carried drinking water for centuries. The second sentence cuts against that expectation by explaining that scale quickly coated the metal, so the water was not sitting against bare lead. A contrast transition is what marks that reversal.

whyWrong.A: "Thus" claims the mineral content of the water was a consequence of using lead pipes, which reverses the actual relationship.
whyWrong.B: The scale layer is not an instance of lead pipes being used; it is a separate fact about the water.
whyWrong.C: "In fact" would intensify or confirm the first sentence, but the second sentence complicates it instead.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim about the instrument's sensitivity — it registers tremors nobody could feel. The second gives one concrete case of that sensitivity, a quarry blast fifty kilometres off. Moving from a general claim to a specific case calls for an illustration transition.

whyWrong.B: Nothing is being contrasted; the second sentence agrees with and illustrates the first.
whyWrong.C: "Instead" would correct or replace the first sentence, but the first sentence is not being withdrawn.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" signals a concession against the first sentence, and detecting a distant blast is not surprising given extreme sensitivity.

whyCorrect: Exposures lasting several minutes are the cause and clamping sitters' heads is the response to that cause — you cannot hold still for minutes unaided. The transition therefore has to point forward from cause to consequence.

whyWrong.A: Nothing has been summarised; the second sentence adds new information rather than closing a discussion.
whyWrong.C: "Even so" concedes a contrast, but clamping subjects follows naturally from long exposures rather than opposing them.
whyWrong.D: "By comparison" sets two things side by side, and only one photographic practice is described.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasise the lengths Coleman went to, so the sentence has to show an obstacle and the effort she made to get around it. Only this choice combines the refusal by American schools, learning a new language, and training abroad, which is the chain of effort the goal asks for.

whyWrong.A: Where and when she earned the licence is an outcome; on its own it shows no obstacle and no effort.
whyWrong.C: This states her historical significance, which is a different goal from showing what she had to do.
whyWrong.D: This gives the obstacle alone, with nothing about what she did in response to it.

whyCorrect: Significance means why the notes mattered afterward. The note that carries that weight is the Bernoulli method being called the first published computer program, and this choice attaches it to the notes themselves.

whyWrong.B: This makes Babbage's engine the subject and reduces Lovelace to someone who wrote about it, which is the opposite of emphasising her contribution.
whyWrong.C: Length is a fact about the notes but says nothing about why they matter.
whyWrong.D: Translating a paper describes the task she was given, not the significance of what she added to it.

whyCorrect: What makes the mechanism remarkable is the combination of its complexity and its isolation in time: at least 30 interlocking gears doing real astronomical prediction, with nothing comparable for a thousand years afterward. This choice puts both facts in one sentence, so the reader sees the sophistication and how far ahead of its era it was.

whyWrong.A: The recovery date is incidental to why the object is impressive, so half the sentence does no work.
whyWrong.C: What it predicted is part of the story, but with no mention of its mechanical complexity or its isolation nothing marks it as extraordinary.
whyWrong.D: The thousand-year gap alone is not meaningful until the reader knows what the device actually did.

whyCorrect: The colon means the second half of the sentence is the evidence for the blank, and that evidence is thirty years of service with almost no maintenance. That is a claim about how well the design lasts, so the blank names lasting power.

whyWrong.A: A simple design may or may not last; the evidence given is about years of service, not about how few parts or steps are involved.
whyWrong.B: "Economy" would need evidence about cost or resources used, and none is offered.
whyWrong.C: Ingenuity is close to the "elegance" the sentence explicitly sets aside, so it undoes the contrast the sentence builds.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, the blank must be the label for whatever the colon introduces.

whyCorrect: The second half of the sentence says it was fifty years before any grower succeeded, so every attempt before that failed. "Uniformly" tells you the blank applies to all the early attempts without exception, and the word that fits is one meaning they failed.

whyWrong.A: Controversy would mean people disagreed about the attempts, but the sentence reports their outcome, not any dispute.
whyWrong.B: Cost is never mentioned, and an expensive attempt could still have succeeded, which contradicts the fifty-year gap.
whyWrong.C: "Profitable" reverses the meaning — the attempts produced no cultivated orchid at all.

whyCorrect: The grasses arrived quickly, and the shrubs are described as those that once dominated the plain, so the shrubs have lost their place to the grasses. The blank needs a word for one thing taking over from another, and "supplanted" means exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "Preserved" says the grasses kept the shrubs in place, which contradicts "once dominated."
whyWrong.B: "Sheltered" would make the grasses protect the shrubs, again leaving the shrubs still there.
whyWrong.D: Resembling the shrubs says something about the grasses' appearance and would not explain the shrubs' decline.

whyCorrect: The sentence tells you what the register contains: angles, distances and bearings, written down in the same hand for thirty years and complete enough to reconstruct a coastline from. That describes an orderly written record of measurements, which is the sense "register" carries here.

whyWrong.B: That sense names a person, but the field book itself is the register, and a book cannot be an official.
whyWrong.C: The musical sense of "register" has no bearing on a book of survey measurements.
whyWrong.D: A tone of writing would be a style; the text is describing the book's contents, and it explicitly says it records no impressions.

whyCorrect: After the colon the sentence explains what was praised: the report laid out its evidence and refused to claim more than the data supported. Honesty about the limits of one's own evidence is candour, so that is the quality the blank names.

whyWrong.A: Novelty would mean the report's ideas were new, but the sentence praises how it handled evidence, not how original it was.
whyWrong.B: Urgency describes pressing importance, which has nothing to do with declining to overstate the data.
whyWrong.C: Brevity concerns length, and setting out evidence for every recommendation suggests the report was not short.

whyCorrect: Track the three sentences in order: conductors ignored her scores, she went on composing and the notebooks sat in a summer house, and in 2009 new owners found the manuscripts. That is a setback, a response to it, and a much later discovery.

whyWrong.B: The text never describes Price's reputation today; it stops at the moment the manuscripts were found.
whyWrong.C: No works are named and no chronology of compositions is given.
whyWrong.D: No question is posed anywhere in the text.

whyCorrect: The text sets an expectation — the team went out to map sediment — reports what they actually saw, parallel ridges running for kilometres, and then names what produced them: icebergs scouring the bottom as the ice sheet collapsed. Purpose questions ask what the whole text does, and this one narrates a surprise and explains it.

whyWrong.A: The collapse of the ice sheet is mentioned only as the cause of the scours; the text makes no claim about how fast it happened.
whyWrong.B: No land deposits appear in the text, so nothing is compared.
whyWrong.C: Sonar is the tool used, but the text never explains how a survey is carried out.

whyCorrect: The text sets two kinds of evidence against each other. The statistical regularities suggest a real language rather than nonsense, while the failure to match any known tongue and the impossible plants pull the other way. The main idea is that the evidence does not settle the question.

whyWrong.A: The illustrations get one clause; nothing says they are the most studied part of the manuscript.
whyWrong.B: "Hoax" is a verdict the text avoids — the language-like regularities are offered as a reason against dismissing it.
whyWrong.C: The text says the opposite: no one has matched the script to a known tongue.

whyCorrect: The key sentence calls the narratives "indispensable and also difficult" and then gives the reason: the interviewers' identity and the subjects' vulnerable position shaped what was said. The main idea has to hold both halves — the evidence is valuable, and the circumstances of its recording affected it.

whyWrong.A: "Deliberately altered" attributes intent the text never claims; it describes conditions shaping the accounts, not falsification.
whyWrong.B: The text diagnoses a problem but recommends nothing about hiring.
whyWrong.C: This drops the word "indispensable" and pushes the caution into near-dismissal, which is stronger than the text.

commonMistakes: Main-idea answers that keep only the criticism and drop the praise (or the reverse) are the most common trap in a two-sided text.

whyCorrect: The curator's whole case is that confident underdrawing is something only the master would produce. If documented workshop copies show underdrawing of comparable confidence, that feature no longer distinguishes master from workshop, and the single piece of evidence supporting the reattribution stops working.

whyWrong.A: An absence of changes between underdrawing and paint is if anything consistent with a copyist following a model, but it does not attack the confidence argument the curator actually makes.
whyWrong.C: A support felled in the master's lifetime is compatible with the panel being a workshop copy made at the time, so it neither helps nor hurts much — and it certainly does not undermine.
whyWrong.D: How many panels of this size the master made says nothing about who drew this one.

whyCorrect: The proposal blames attention, not the way memory stores order. Attention is something a participant can redirect; a storage mechanism is not. So if simply warning people to attend to the middle raises middle recall to the level of the ends, the deficit was an attention effect, exactly as proposed.

whyWrong.A: A stronger effect in long lists is predicted by both explanations and so distinguishes neither.
whyWrong.C: Appearing at all ages says the effect is general; it says nothing about which of the two causes produces it.
whyWrong.D: Best recall for the last item is simply a restatement of the pattern being explained, not evidence about its cause.

whyCorrect: Two features occur together in the alloy — fine grains and trace niobium — and the scientist credits the grains. The finding that separates them is one that holds niobium constant and varies grain size. Same niobium, coarser grains, far fewer cycles to failure shows the grain structure is doing the work.

whyWrong.B: Having the finest grain structure of any comparable alloy describes the alloy; it never links grain size to the fatigue result.
whyWrong.C: Castability is a manufacturing property and has nothing to do with why the alloy resists fatigue.
whyWrong.D: Production cost is irrelevant to the mechanism being argued about.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes the mechanism: heat lowers a panel's efficiency. The experiment then shows that panels raised a few centimetres, so air can move underneath, produce more power than identical flush-mounted panels. Air moving beneath a panel carries heat away, so the conclusion that follows is that mounting height works through cooling.

whyWrong.A: The test compared identical panels, so it holds the efficiency rating fixed and gives no basis for ranking height against rating.
whyWrong.C: Wind loading is never discussed, and the finding favours raising panels, not minimising the gap.
whyWrong.D: The panels in the test were in desert sun above their rated temperature and still showed a measurable difference.

whyCorrect: The text sets up a contrast marked by "by contrast": the animal's appearance has barely changed, but molecular studies show its DNA accumulating changes faster than that of any other vertebrate measured. The completion must state the genome side of that contrast, which is rapid change hidden behind a stable outward form.

whyWrong.A: This repeats the appearance side of the contrast and directly contradicts the molecular finding.
whyWrong.C: Similarity to other reptiles is not what the studies measured; they measured the rate at which changes accumulated.
whyWrong.D: The text says the comparison has already been made — faster than any other vertebrate yet measured.

whyCorrect: "A kingdom centred on what is now northern Ethiopia" is an appositive renaming Aksum, and it is already opened with a comma after "Aksum." A non-essential element dropped into the middle of a sentence needs the same mark at both ends, so a second comma has to close it before the verb "minted."

whyWrong.A: A colon breaks the subject away from its verb, and the material after it is not an explanation or list.
whyWrong.B: With no closing punctuation the appositive is left open, so the sentence reads as though the phrase never ended.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and "minted its own coinage from the third century onward" has no subject of its own.

tips: An interrupter opened with a comma must be closed with a comma — check the mark on both sides, not just the one nearest the blank.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence, and everything after it is a list naming the species just referred to. A colon is the mark that introduces a list after a complete clause.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and "dormice, several warblers and a great many invertebrates" is only a list of nouns.
whyWrong.B: "But" signals a contrast, and the list names the very species the first clause says hedgerows shelter, so there is nothing to contrast.
whyWrong.C: "And" would make the list a second item joined to the first clause, which garbles the meaning — the species are the examples, not an additional thing hedgerows do.

whyCorrect: "When the tide is out" is a dependent clause because of "When," and it comes first, so it is joined to the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.A: Adding "that" leaves the sentence with no main clause — "When the tide is out that the causeway is passable" never resolves into a statement.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs two independent clauses, and the "When" clause is not one.
whyWrong.D: A colon also requires a complete independent clause in front of it.

whyCorrect: "Although" makes the first clause dependent, so it cannot be joined to the main clause by anything that requires two complete sentences. A leading dependent clause takes a comma.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon demands an independent clause on both sides, and "Although the manuscript is undated" is not one.
whyWrong.C: A colon likewise needs a complete clause before it.
whyWrong.D: "Although" and "and" pull in opposite directions, and using "and" leaves the "Although" clause with nothing to attach to.

whyCorrect: The sentence criticises the ministry "for failing to consult residents and for _____." Both items follow the same preposition "for," so they must take the same form, and the first is the gerund "failing." The parallel form is "ignoring."

whyWrong.A: "For it ignored" puts a full clause after a preposition, which does not work and breaks the parallel with "failing."
whyWrong.B: "Having ignore" is not a legal form; the perfect gerund would be "having ignored," and even then it would not match "failing."
whyWrong.C: "For to ignore" is ungrammatical, and an infinitive does not pair with the gerund "failing."

whyCorrect: The sentence has two past moments: the packing in September and the arrival at the coast, which is itself in the past. The depletion happened before the later past event, so it takes the past perfect, and the supplies were acted on rather than acting, so the passive is right: "had been depleted."

whyWrong.A: "Deplete" is present tense and active, so it both clashes with the past-tense frame and makes the supplies do the depleting.
whyWrong.C: "Will be depleted" is future, which cannot describe something already true when the expedition arrived.
whyWrong.D: "Are depleted" is present tense and places the state now rather than before the past arrival.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The collection," a singular noun. "Along with several atlases" is an interrupting phrase set off by commas, and phrases like "along with," "as well as" and "in addition to" never change the number of the subject. So the verb stays singular: "is kept."

whyWrong.B: "Have been" is plural, agreeing with "atlases" inside the interrupter rather than with "collection."
whyWrong.C: "Were" is plural and also shifts the sentence into the past for no reason.
whyWrong.D: "Are" is plural and disagrees with the singular subject "collection."

commonMistakes: Treating "along with X" as if it were "and X" — only "and" creates a compound plural subject.

whyCorrect: The first sentence lists advantages: light and unusually stiff. The second gives a drawback that limits where the alloy can be used. Moving from a strength to an offsetting weakness calls for a contrast transition.

whyWrong.B: "Therefore" would make the high price a consequence of being light and stiff, but the second sentence restricts use rather than following from those properties.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" adds a similar point, and expense is not similar to lightness and stiffness.
whyWrong.D: The cost is not an example of the alloy's mechanical properties.

whyCorrect: The fire destroyed the colony's own records, which is why historians have to rely on letters kept somewhere else. The second sentence states the result of the first, so a cause-and-effect transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" marks a result that defies expectation, but relying on outside letters is exactly what you would expect after the local records burned.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is being set against anything else; there is one archive and one consequence.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" would introduce a parallel case, and no second colony or archive is mentioned.

whyCorrect: Both sentences describe an animal surviving deep cold by an extreme physiological measure — frogs by freezing nearly solid, fish by making proteins that block ice formation. The second is another instance of the same phenomenon, so an addition transition marking likeness fits.

whyWrong.A: The fish strategy is not caused by what the frogs do; the two are independent adaptations.
whyWrong.B: "In other words" restates the previous sentence, but the second sentence introduces a different animal and a different mechanism.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" signals that the second statement holds despite the first, and there is no tension between the two.

commonMistakes: Different mechanisms can still be parallel examples; "similarly" tracks the role two facts play, not whether their details match.

whyCorrect: Technical skill has to be shown by an outcome that skill produced. The notes supply one: brick fitted tightly and sealed with bitumen that has held water for over four thousand years. This choice states both the construction method and the result that proves it worked.

whyWrong.A: A construction date and an unresolved debate about purpose say nothing about how well the thing was built.
whyWrong.C: The tight brickwork alone is the method with no evidence of how well it performed, so the skill is asserted rather than demonstrated.
whyWrong.D: The debate over purpose is a different topic entirely.

whyCorrect: Sharing a cost requires both a cost and a mechanism that spreads it. The cost is the heat loss on the windward edge, and the mechanism is the slow inward shuffle that eventually puts every bird there for a similar stretch. This choice links the two in one sentence.

whyWrong.A: That penguins huddle is background; it does not explain how the burden is distributed.
whyWrong.C: This names the cost but leaves out the movement that shares it, so it explains nothing about fairness.
whyWrong.D: This describes the movement without saying what it accomplishes for the birds on the edge.

whyCorrect: Lasting influence means reaching beyond the patent's own moment. Only this choice carries the story forward to Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and setting that against the navy's refusal sharpens the point that the idea outlived its rejection.

whyWrong.A: This stops in 1942 with the original military purpose and never reaches any later use.
whyWrong.B: The navy's refusal is the opposite of influence unless it is paired with the later adoption.
whyWrong.D: This restates the wartime intention only, with no mention of anything the patent later shaped.

whyCorrect: The semicolon introduces the evidence: she accepted the claim only after hours of her own footage. "Only after" means acceptance was withheld until then, so her initial position was doubt. "Sceptical" names that doubt about a claim.

whyWrong.A: Indifference is not caring either way, but she cared enough to watch hours of footage and to change her mind.
whyWrong.B: Being informed about a claim says nothing about whether she believed it, and it leaves the "only after" contrast with nothing to reverse.
whyWrong.C: "Adamant" means unshakeable, which contradicts the fact that she did change her mind — and the sentence does not say which position she would have been adamant about.

whyCorrect: The "so … that" structure makes the second half the measure of the blank: a week of work covers only a fraction of the material on one decade. That is a statement about sheer quantity, so the blank has to describe size.

whyWrong.A: A specialised archive is narrow in subject, which would tend to mean less material, not more than a researcher can get through.
whyWrong.B: Fragility would restrict handling, but the sentence measures how much there is to examine, not how carefully it must be treated.
whyWrong.C: Disorganisation could slow a researcher down, but the sentence says the researcher examines only a fraction of the material, which points to volume rather than to difficulty finding things.

whyCorrect: "But" makes the ink analysis the correction to the old dismissal, and what that analysis establishes is that the diaries really date from the period they describe. The charge it refutes must therefore be that they were fakes written later, which is what "fraudulent" means.

whyWrong.A: Ink dating tells you when the diaries were written, not whether anything is missing from them.
whyWrong.B: "Derivative" would mean they copied other sources, a charge the date of the ink cannot answer.
whyWrong.D: Triviality is a judgement about importance, and no chemical test could overturn it.

tips: In a "once dismissed as X, but evidence Y" sentence, work backwards from what Y actually proves.

whyCorrect: Two teams published within weeks of each other, so neither can be given sole credit. The blank describes what convention now does with the discovery in relation to both teams, and "attributed to both" says the credit is assigned to each of them.

whyWrong.A: "Confined to both" is self-contradictory — confinement restricts to one, and there are two teams.
whyWrong.B: "Opposed to both" would set the discovery against the teams that made it.
whyWrong.C: "Referred to both" is not idiomatic for credit; you refer a matter to someone for a decision, which is not what happened here.

whyCorrect: The phrase after the comma spells out the criticism: the proposal treats the symptoms of overcrowding and leaves its causes alone. A response that stops at the visible surface of a problem is superficial.

whyWrong.B: Cost is never mentioned, and an expensive plan could still reach the causes.
whyWrong.C: "Premature" would mean it came too early, but the objection is about what the proposal covers, not about its timing.
whyWrong.D: Unpopularity is about how people received it, whereas the criticism given concerns what it fails to address.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence makes a bare assertion — lichens are not single organisms — and the two sentences after it supply the substance behind it: each lichen is a partnership of two organisms with complementary contributions. The sentence sets up the claim, and the rest of the text explains it.

whyWrong.A: No objection is raised; the sentence states the text's own position, and nothing afterwards disputes it.
whyWrong.B: It gives no example — "lichens" is the general subject of the whole text, and the definition follows it rather than preceding it.
whyWrong.C: It introduces the generalisation instead of qualifying one; the text contains no earlier or later claim that it narrows.

whyCorrect: The text opens by naming the standard account, which starts with Gutenberg, then reports evidence against it — movable type in Korea two centuries earlier — and closes by saying precisely what Europe did contribute: metallurgy cheap enough to make type disposable. Naming a received account and then replacing it with a more exact claim is a correction.

whyWrong.A: The text does not deflate Gutenberg; it identifies a real European innovation and credits it.
whyWrong.B: Bronze versus lead alloy is one detail used in the argument, not the point of the text.
whyWrong.D: No route of transmission is described; the text does not claim Europe learned printing from Korea.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence rules out one function — the bower holds no eggs and is abandoned after breeding — and the last sentence supplies another: females compare bowers, and males stripped of decorations are chosen less. Put together, the bower serves in attracting a mate, not in rearing young.

whyWrong.B: The text says decorations are sorted by colour, which is not the same as females preferring a single colour; no preference for one colour is reported.
whyWrong.C: Removing decorations was an experiment used as evidence, and the text does not claim breeding was disrupted overall.
whyWrong.D: The text explicitly denies that the bower is a nest, and body size is never mentioned.

whyCorrect: The text traces the chain otters to urchins to kelp, shows the collapse when otters were removed, and then reports recovery within a decade when they return — but the final clause adds a condition, that the rock still holds sediment for young kelp to anchor in. The main idea has to include that condition, not just the recovery.

whyWrong.A: "Sole cause" is stronger than the text, which adds substrate as a second factor limiting recovery.
whyWrong.B: The text never compares otters with other predators or claims they are the only one that works.
whyWrong.D: No other grazer is discussed, so no comparison of damage is available.

commonMistakes: A final "but only where…" clause is usually the point of the passage, not a footnote to it.

whyCorrect: Warmth and traffic nitrogen normally travel together in cities, so the finding that helps has to separate them. Cool coastal cities have the traffic but not the extra warmth, and if their street trees grow no faster than nearby rural trees, then nitrogen alone is not producing the effect — the warmth is what is missing.

whyWrong.A: Taller city trees at the same age is the very pattern both explanations were invented to account for, so it favours neither.
whyWrong.C: Higher nitrogen in city soils supports the rival explanation, not Lindqvist's.
whyWrong.D: Rural trees beside motorways get exhaust nitrogen without a city's warmth, and their growing faster is evidence for the nitrogen account.

tips: To choose between two explanations for one pattern, find the case where the two causes come apart.

whyCorrect: The argument has one step: small hands, therefore adolescents. That step assumes adult hands in this population were larger than the stencils. If adult women's hands fell within the same size range, the size evidence no longer picks out adolescents and the inference collapses.

whyWrong.A: A span of centuries tells you when the stencils were made, not the age of whoever made them.
whyWrong.C: Similar stencils elsewhere extends the practice geographically without saying anything about hand size or age.
whyWrong.D: Where the pigment came from concerns trade, not the identity of the artists.

whyCorrect: The historian is ruling out one local cause, more wool, in favour of an external one, changed trade routes. Sheep numbers holding steady across the period means the countryside was not producing more wool, which removes the rival explanation and leaves the trade-route account standing.

whyWrong.A: Rising wool exports are compatible with either story and, taken alone, look more like evidence for the local-production explanation the historian rejects.
whyWrong.C: Growth over the following century describes what happened afterwards, not what caused the sudden prosperity.
whyWrong.D: Neighbouring towns prospering too is suggestive but does not distinguish the causes — they might all have raised more sheep.

whyCorrect: The text splits the comparison in two: full sun wins on beans per hectare, while shade wins on soil nitrogen, erosion and how long the plot keeps producing. A grower who looks only at yield sees the first column and none of the second, so the durability advantage of shade is invisible and full sun looks better over the long run than it is.

whyWrong.A: Yield alone favours full sun, so a yield-only comparison would not make shade look more profitable in any season.
whyWrong.B: Ignoring soil quality is not the same as concluding there is no effect; the grower simply never weighs it.
whyWrong.C: Full-sun yield is the one thing such a grower measures accurately, so it would not be underestimated.

whyCorrect: Two details drive the inference: the gifts are meticulously recorded, and a family that receives one is expected to return an equivalent at a later wedding. A recorded transfer of value that must be repaid later is a loan in all but name, which is why the practice is less generosity than credit between families.

whyWrong.A: The families track the amounts and know what is owed, so the meaning is anything but forgotten.
whyWrong.B: No religious authority appears in the text; the obligation runs between families.
whyWrong.D: Matching the value of what was received is the opposite of competitive display, which would require outdoing the other family.

whyCorrect: "The library holds three items of interest to the project" is a complete sentence, and what follows names those three items. A colon after a complete clause is the standard way to introduce a list, and the commas inside the list then separate its members.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs a full independent clause on its right, but "a ledger, a bundle of letters and a hand-drawn plan" is a string of noun phrases.
whyWrong.C: "And" turns the ledger into a fourth thing added to the three items rather than the first of them, which contradicts the count.
whyWrong.D: "To the project which are a ledger" attaches the relative clause to "the project" instead of to "three items," producing a plural verb with a singular antecedent and no punctuation to separate the clause.

whyCorrect: "The survey covered every district in the city" and "the results were published the following spring" are each complete sentences, and no conjunction is offered. Two independent clauses in that situation take a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the two clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: A colon signals that what follows explains or specifies what came before, but a later publication date is a separate fact, not an elaboration of the survey's coverage.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone as sentences: the engine ran for eleven hours, and then it seized. "Then" is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot join clauses on its own — a semicolon is required.

whyWrong.A: A colon promises an explanation or specification of the first clause, but the seizure is a later event rather than an unpacking of the eleven fault-free hours.
whyWrong.B: Without any mark the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.D: A comma before "then" leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma and an adverb, which is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Treating "then," "however" and "therefore" as conjunctions; they are adverbs, and a comma before them between two clauses still splices.

whyCorrect: "The smallest planet in the solar system" is an appositive describing Mercury, and it is already opened by the comma after "Mercury." A non-essential phrase inside a sentence needs matching punctuation at both ends, so a comma has to close it before the verb "has."

whyWrong.A: A colon separates the subject from its verb and introduces nothing that needs introducing.
whyWrong.B: Leaving the appositive unclosed runs it into the verb, so the sentence never signals where the interrupting phrase ends.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, and "has almost no atmosphere to retain heat" has no subject.

whyCorrect: With "neither … nor," the verb agrees with whichever subject is closer to it. Here the nearer subject is "the two assistants," which is plural, and the sentence is set in the past, so the verb is "were."

whyWrong.A: "Has been" is singular, agreeing with "surveyor" instead of the nearer plural subject, and the present perfect clashes with the finished past event.
whyWrong.B: "Is" is both singular and present tense.
whyWrong.C: "Was" has the right tense but the wrong number for the nearer subject "assistants."

whyCorrect: The sentence gives two past times, March and June, and the writing of the recommendations into policy was finished by the later one. An action completed before a stated past point takes the past perfect, and the recommendations were written rather than doing the writing, so the passive is required: "had been written."

whyWrong.A: "Are written" is present tense and cannot describe something already complete by a past June.
whyWrong.B: "Have written" is active, which makes the recommendations write themselves into policy, and its tense does not sit behind the past-tense frame.
whyWrong.D: "Writing" is a participle with no auxiliary, leaving the second clause without a finite verb.

whyCorrect: The opening participial phrase, "Having been restored twice in the last century," is a modifier, not a clause. The main clause that follows still needs a finite verb for the subject "the fresco," and "shows" supplies it.

whyWrong.B: "To show" is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence.
whyWrong.C: "Shown" is a past participle with no auxiliary, so the sentence stays a fragment.
whyWrong.D: "Showing" adds a second participle to a sentence that already opens with one, leaving no main verb at all.

whyCorrect: A faster journey should attract riders, so the fall in passenger numbers runs against what the first sentence leads you to expect. A concessive transition is what marks a result that holds despite that expectation.

whyWrong.A: "That is" restates the previous sentence in other words, but falling ridership is new and different information.
whyWrong.B: "Accordingly" makes the drop a consequence of the shorter journey, which reverses the expected effect.
whyWrong.D: "Indeed" strengthens or confirms the prior sentence, and a decline does not confirm an improvement.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a good reason to build on ridgelines; the second says migrating birds use the same ridgelines. The two facts collide, and the transition has to flag that the coincidence is a problem.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" adds a parallel point, but bird migration routes are not a second reason to site turbines on ridges.
whyWrong.B: Birds did not start following ridgelines because turbines were built there, so this is not a result.
whyWrong.C: "In particular" narrows the previous statement to a specific case, and the second sentence changes subject to birds instead.

whyCorrect: Shared errors in the same places are the evidence, and a common exemplar is the conclusion drawn from that evidence — identical mistakes are hard to explain by chance. The transition therefore has to signal an inference.

whyWrong.A: "Admittedly" concedes a point against the writer's position, but the second sentence is the position.
whyWrong.B: "Conversely" introduces an opposite case, and the second sentence follows from the first rather than opposing it.
whyWrong.D: "Meanwhile" marks simultaneous events, which is not the relationship between evidence and conclusion.

whyCorrect: An exchange needs both directions stated. The notes give sugars going from tree to fungus and phosphorus going from fungus to tree, and this choice names both, along with the hyphae that carry them.

whyWrong.A: This describes the physical connection only, with nothing passing in either direction.
whyWrong.B: Saying both benefit asserts the outcome without naming what either side actually gives.
whyWrong.D: This covers one direction and leaves the tree's contribution out, so it is not an exchange.

whyCorrect: Economic importance needs a measure of value, and the notes contain exactly one: for two centuries cochineal ranked second only to silver among Mexico's exports. That comparison shows the scale of the trade.

whyWrong.A: What the dye is made from is a fact about its production, not its economic weight.
whyWrong.B: An export route and a start date establish that trade existed without saying how much it was worth.
whyWrong.D: Being replaced by synthetic dyes marks the end of the trade rather than its importance while it lasted.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain a mechanism, so the sentence has to run the whole chain: roots trap sediment, trapped sediment raises the seabed, and a raised seabed lowers the waves that reach the shore. This choice keeps all three links in order.

whyWrong.A: This gives the setting only and never reaches the effect on waves.
whyWrong.C: Trapping sediment is the first step, but with the seabed and the waves left out the protection is never explained.
whyWrong.D: This states the outcome with no mechanism, so it does not show how mangroves produce it.

whyCorrect: The colon introduces two results joined by "yet": repayment beat every expectation, but incomes rose no faster than in villages that got nothing. One finding is good and the other is not, so the blank has to name a result that points both ways at once.

whyWrong.B: "Damning" covers only the disappointing half and ignores the repayment rates the designers had not dared hope for.
whyWrong.C: "Conclusive" would mean the evaluations settled the question, but two findings pulling in opposite directions settle nothing.
whyWrong.D: "Enthusiastic" describes a reaction rather than a result, and it fits only the repayment half.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets "not a picturesque survival" against the blank, so the blank must mean the opposite of a mere charming relic — something that actually works now. The first sentence supplies the reason: the towers cool rooms with no moving parts and no electricity. "Viable" says the design is a workable solution to a current problem.

whyWrong.A: "Decorative" is a synonym for the "picturesque" half the sentence rejects, so it destroys the contrast.
whyWrong.B: Nothing suggests the towers are a stopgap; the point is that they have worked for centuries and still work.
whyWrong.C: "Traditional" repeats the "survival" idea rather than opposing it, and the sentence needs a word about present usefulness.

commonMistakes: With "not X but _____," the blank must contrast with X; choosing a near-synonym of X is the most common slip.

whyCorrect: The colon explains what is admired, and both examples describe the listener's expectations being defeated — a phrase starts where silence was expected and ends before the line sounds complete. The blank names that quality of confounding expectation.

whyWrong.A: Brevity is about length overall; the examples are about placement and timing relative to what the listener anticipates, and one of them describes a phrase starting early rather than being short.
whyWrong.C: Precision would mean the playing lands exactly where expected, the reverse of both examples.
whyWrong.D: Warmth describes tone or emotional quality, which neither example touches.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes the timing: virus fragments appear in sewage several days before patients appear in clinics. Wastewater sampling therefore signals an outbreak before case counts can, so the warning it gives comes early.

whyWrong.A: "Reluctant" describes an unwilling person, and a warning cannot be unwilling.
whyWrong.B: "Belated" means late, which reverses the several-day lead the first sentence establishes.
whyWrong.D: "Ambiguous" would make the warning unclear, but the sentence praises the method for beating case counts, not for being hard to read.

whyCorrect: The officers fought on opposite sides and agreed on nothing else, so neither had any reason to echo the other and their accounts are independent. When two hostile, independent witnesses converge on the same detail, that detail becomes hard to dismiss — the agreement carries unusual weight as evidence.

whyWrong.A: Ambiguity would mean the accounts are unclear, but they state the same hour plainly.
whyWrong.B: Suspicion would be warranted if the two had reason to coordinate; opposing sides that agree on nothing else is precisely the condition that removes that worry.
whyWrong.D: "Incidental" would make the agreement a side detail of no consequence, which the word "especially" and the setup both work against.

whyCorrect: The first sentence implies that camera and radar cover each other's blind spots, which makes combining them sound straightforward. The underlined sentence pushes back — the sensors contradict each other, so choosing which to trust is itself a problem — and the final sentence gives the industry's answer, weighting each sensor by how reliable it has proved in current conditions. The sentence complicates the implied advantage and prepares the solution.

whyWrong.A: It ranks neither sensor; the point is that the two disagree, not that one is generally better.
whyWrong.B: No technical term is defined, and none was introduced earlier.
whyWrong.C: It adds a new difficulty rather than restating the complementary strengths already described.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence states the fact the scheme was designed around: planting is cheap and keeping a tree alive is not. The following sentence spells out how the design answers it — payment on survival puts the money where the difficulty lies — and the last reports the result. So the sentence names the insight that the whole programme rests on.

whyWrong.A: It raises no doubt about the count; the thirty million figure appears later and is not challenged.
whyWrong.B: Techniques of planting are never described for either Maathai or professional foresters; the contrast is about what the payment rewards.
whyWrong.C: The women's motives are addressed by the payment structure, not by this sentence, which is about a cost fact the foresters missed.

whyCorrect: The puzzle set up in the first sentence is that nutrients wash out of Amazonian soil about as fast as decay releases them. The dust from Chad delivers phosphorus, and satellite estimates put the yearly delivery at roughly what the rivers remove. So the dust makes up the losses.

whyWrong.A: The text names phosphorus specifically; nitrogen is never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: The rivers carry nutrients away, but the text says the dust settles over the basin as an input, not that it is exported.
whyWrong.D: Sunlight and rainfall are not discussed anywhere in the passage.

whyCorrect: The question asks what the text reports for several districts, and the text says the income gap between large and small farms widened as the new seed spread. The reason given is that the new varieties needed irrigation and yearly fertiliser purchases that the smallest holdings could not reliably afford.

whyWrong.B: The text says gains in output were real and never claims any farm's harvest fell below its earlier level.
whyWrong.C: Fertiliser prices are not discussed; the problem stated is that small farms could not afford it, not that it became cheaper.
whyWrong.D: No abandonment is reported — the seed spread rather than being given up.

whyCorrect: The conservator's case rests on the assumption that the wet-into-wet shadow technique is personal enough to identify one painter. If apprentices in that very workshop were trained to lay in shadow exactly as the master did, the identical technique on both halves is equally consistent with two hands, and the evidence stops distinguishing one painter from two.

whyWrong.A: When the book was bound bears on the manuscript's assembly, not on how many painters worked on the page.
whyWrong.B: Wide variation between workshops actually helps the conservator, since it makes a shared technique more distinctive.
whyWrong.D: A common pigment source shows the two halves were painted in one workshop with the same materials, which is true whether one painter or two did the work.

commonMistakes: To weaken a "only one person could have done this" argument, show that someone else could have done it too — not that the evidence is real.

whyCorrect: Two causes ran at the same time in the same city, so the useful evidence is a case where they come apart. Neighbouring cities whose fleets turned over at the same rate but which imposed no charge recorded no comparable fall — fleet turnover held constant, the charge absent, and the improvement gone with it. That leaves the charge as the factor doing the work.

whyWrong.A: That diesels emit more nitrogen dioxide than petrol engines is background that supports the rival fleet-turnover explanation if anything.
whyWrong.C: A bigger drop in year two shows the fall continued, but the old diesels were leaving the fleet across those same years, so it separates nothing.
whyWrong.D: Fewer vehicles entering the zone shows the charge changed traffic, but not that the pollution fall came from that rather than from cleaner vehicles nationally.

whyCorrect: The sociolinguist has to rule out deliberate maintenance as a badge of identity, and deliberate maintenance requires that speakers know their vowels mark them out. If islanders asked about their vowels do not even realise they differ from mainland speech, the identity explanation has nothing to stand on, and the passive explanation — isolation — is what remains.

whyWrong.A: Older speakers using the system more consistently describes change now under way and says nothing about why it survived for two centuries.
whyWrong.B: Boat-only access suggests isolation, but a fishing community owns boats, so this establishes how the island was reached rather than that contact was rare — and it leaves the identity explanation untouched.
whyWrong.C: Survivals on other islands show the pattern is not unique without indicating which of the two causes produced any of them.

tips: When a claim is "because X, not because Y," a finding that makes Y impossible supports it as directly as one that confirms X.

whyCorrect: The text describes a detection bias, not a fact about planets: big close-in planets make deep, frequent dips and are confirmed within months, while small distant ones may transit once a decade at the very limit of instrument sensitivity. A catalogue built from such surveys therefore fills up with the easy cases, so its proportions do not match what is actually out there.

whyWrong.A: "No planets smaller than Earth" is far stronger than the text, which says small distant planets are hard to detect, not impossible.
whyWrong.B: Stellar brightness is never mentioned; the two variables discussed are planet size and orbital period.
whyWrong.C: Systems resembling our own contain small planets on wide orbits, which are exactly the ones these surveys miss.

commonMistakes: A sampling bias means the catalogue misrepresents proportions, not that whole classes of object are absent.

whyCorrect: The pigment was first manufactured in the 1820s, and it sits evenly through the preparatory ground beneath the paint rather than in a patch of retouching. A ground layer is laid before the picture is painted, so the panel's preparation cannot predate the pigment's existence — whatever the signature says, the preparation is nineteenth-century or later.

whyWrong.B: The text rules retouching out explicitly by noting the pigment is not in a retouched patch but distributed through the ground.
whyWrong.C: Attribution to a different artist is a further inference; all the evidence establishes is a date, and that date already contradicts the 1631 inscription without telling you who painted it.
whyWrong.D: A cataloguing error concerns record-keeping, and the analysis speaks to the object itself rather than to how it was recorded.

whyCorrect: Everything up to the blank is governed by "After," which makes it a dependent clause no matter how long it runs. A dependent clause placed in front of the main clause is joined to it with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and the "After" clause is not one.
whyWrong.B: A colon likewise requires an independent clause before it.
whyWrong.C: "And" would join two equal elements, but the first is dependent, so the sentence never delivers a main clause.

commonMistakes: Length is not the test — a long word group beginning with "After," "Because" or "When" is still dependent.

whyCorrect: "All of which were waterlogged and had to be stabilised" is a relative clause built on "which," so it must stay attached to the list of objects it describes rather than standing alone. A comma is what attaches a non-essential relative clause.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and a "which" clause cannot function as a sentence.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces a list or an explanation; this is a modifier of the nouns already listed.
whyWrong.C: A period leaves a fragment, and the lowercase "all" shows the clause was not written to begin a sentence.

whyCorrect: "The mycologist catalogued more than four hundred specimens in a single field season" and "fewer than a dozen had ever been recorded in the region before her survey began" are both complete sentences, and no coordinating conjunction is supplied. That combination requires a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by "and" doubles the connector; either mark alone might work, but not the pair.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences — the kiln fires at a lower temperature, and it produces a crazing-resistant glaze. Joining two independent clauses takes either a semicolon or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, and this choice supplies the comma and "and."

whyWrong.A: The semicolon is legal, but "also it also produces" says "also" twice, which is not English.
whyWrong.B: Without any mark between them the clauses run together.
whyWrong.D: A comma with no conjunction between independent clauses is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: The possessor is "the committee," a singular collective noun acting as one body, so the possessive pronoun is the singular "its." The mention of individual dissenting members does not change the number of the noun the pronoun refers back to.

whyWrong.A: "Their" is plural and does not agree with the singular "committee."
whyWrong.C: "It's" is the contraction of "it is," which cannot show possession.
whyWrong.D: "They're" is the contraction of "they are" and is not a possessive at all.

whyCorrect: "Ever since" describes an action that began in the past and is still going on, which is what the present perfect expresses. The museum acquired the drawing and has displayed it from then up to now.

whyWrong.B: The simple present "displays" reports a current fact and cannot carry the stretch of time "ever since" requires.
whyWrong.C: The past perfect places the display before some other past event, but no such later event is given — the period runs up to the present.
whyWrong.D: "Will display" is future and contradicts a display that has already been going on since the acquisition.

whyCorrect: "Both … and" must join two items of the same grammatical kind, and the first is the adjective phrase "effective at low doses." The second has to be an adjective phrase too, so "safe over long periods of use" is the match.

whyWrong.A: "It was safe" is a full clause, which cannot pair with the adjective phrase after "both."
whyWrong.B: "Safely" is an adverb, and the sentence needs an adjective describing the compound, not a manner of doing something.
whyWrong.D: "Being safe" is a gerund phrase, which does not match the adjective on the other side of "and."

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the physical cause: sea water absorbs low-frequency sound far less than air does. The second gives the effect that follows — a twenty-hertz call still audible hundreds of kilometres away. That is a cause-to-effect link.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" would mark the second fact as surprising given the first, but long-range travel is exactly what low absorption predicts.
whyWrong.B: "By comparison" needs two things set side by side, and the second sentence gives a consequence rather than a second case.
whyWrong.C: "Admittedly" concedes a point against the writer's argument, and nothing here is being conceded.

whyCorrect: Both sentences describe colour produced by physical structure instead of by pigment — nanoscale crystals in chameleon skin, scale structure in a morpho wing. The second is a second instance of the same principle, so the transition should mark likeness.

whyWrong.B: "However" signals contrast, but the butterfly agrees with the chameleon rather than opposing it.
whyWrong.C: The butterfly's colour is not caused by anything the chameleon does, so this is not a consequence.
whyWrong.D: "Instead" would replace the first statement with a correction, and the first statement is not being withdrawn.

whyCorrect: The first sentence lists disadvantages of writing by hand: it is slower and captures less of the lecture. The second reports that hand-writers nevertheless do better on conceptual questions a week later. The result runs against what the drawbacks lead you to expect, so a concessive transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: "Accordingly" makes better recall a consequence of capturing less, which is the opposite of what the first sentence implies.
whyWrong.C: "That is" restates the previous sentence, and a test result a week later is new evidence, not a rewording.
whyWrong.D: The test outcome is not an example of note-taking being slow or less complete.

whyCorrect: The task asks for one advantage and one drawback in the same sentence. The water saving is the advantage and the dominant lighting cost is the drawback, and this choice joins them with "though," which marks the second as a qualification of the first.

whyWrong.A: This gives the advantage alone, so half the task is missing.
whyWrong.C: Stacking trays and being near cities are descriptive facts, neither presented as a benefit or a cost.
whyWrong.D: This gives the drawback alone, with no advantage to set against it.

whyCorrect: An arid climate makes water scarce and evaporation costly, so the explanation has to name the features that answer those pressures. This choice states all three: the tunnel runs underground so little water evaporates, gravity moves the water so no fuel or pump is needed, and it reaches the village from a highland aquifer.

whyWrong.A: Longevity shows the design endured but does not say what about it suits dry conditions.
whyWrong.C: Gravity flow alone leaves out the evaporation saving, which is the feature that matters most where water is scarce.
whyWrong.D: This defines what a qanat is without explaining any advantage.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain a mechanism, so the sentence must connect the pond to the fire risk through the intermediate steps. This choice keeps the chain intact: ponds raise the water table, the raised table keeps vegetation green into the dry season, and green vegetation resists burning.

whyWrong.A: The greener vegetation is stated without the water table that causes it or the fire consequence that follows, so nothing is explained.
whyWrong.B: This jumps from ponds straight to flammability, leaving out the water table and the greener vegetation that connect them.
whyWrong.D: Seepage is one link in the chain and stops well short of any effect on fire.

whyCorrect: The colon lists what the dance conveys: the angle of the straight run gives direction relative to the sun, and its length gives distance to within a few metres. Both details are about how much a watching bee learns, so the blank has to describe the dance as a carrier of information.

whyWrong.A: "Laborious" would describe how much effort the dance costs the bee, and the colon says nothing about effort.
whyWrong.B: "Erratic" means irregular, which contradicts a code precise enough to specify distance within a few metres.
whyWrong.C: "Ornamental" means decorative and without function, the opposite of a display that transmits usable directions.

whyCorrect: The second sentence says what each new cohort added: a consistent word order and grammatical markers the first signers did without. Those additions build structure onto a simpler system, so the blank has to mean more developed and complex.

whyWrong.B: Adding fixed word order and grammatical markers makes a system more regulated, not more informal.
whyWrong.C: "Widespread" is about how many people use it; the sentence describes changes to the system itself.
whyWrong.D: The system was invented at the school within a few years, so nothing about it can become ancient.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets up the need: no existing term fitted her find. The next tells you what she produced — a word welded together from two Greek roots that struck colleagues as ugly. She made a new word, so "coin" here means to invent.

whyWrong.A: Borrowing from another field would mean the term already existed, and the text says no term in the literature fitted.
whyWrong.C: Minting currency is the literal, financial sense of the word and has nothing to do with naming a geological feature.
whyWrong.D: Translating would mean rendering an existing term in another language, but she built a new word out of roots.

whyCorrect: The passage is about slowing water: marsh grass makes water move at a fraction of channel speed, and that delay stops a surge before it reaches the town. "Check" here names what the delay does to the surge, which is hold it back.

whyWrong.B: Marking with a tick is the clerical sense and makes no sense applied to a surge of water.
whyWrong.C: Inspecting is an act of examination, and wetlands do not examine floodwater.
whyWrong.D: Verifying belongs to the same checking-for-accuracy family and has nothing to do with reducing a flood.

tips: For an underlined-word question, substitute your candidate into the sentence and check that the surrounding logic still runs.

whyCorrect: The repairer does not hide the break; gold-dusted lacquer makes it "the first thing the eye follows." That phrase defines the blank as being about visibility, so the word needed means standing out to the eye.

whyWrong.A: The break may well be the most recent thing that happened to the bowl, but recency is not what draws the eye, and the sentence is about how the repair looks.
whyWrong.C: A repaired and filled crack is not presented as the weakest point, and fragility is not something the eye follows.
whyWrong.D: Value is a judgement about worth; the sentence describes what the viewer notices first.

whyCorrect: Follow the four sentences: a satellite measuring ozone, a ground station measuring the same thing, a conflict when the ground readings dropped while the satellite showed nothing, and finally the cause — software written to discard implausibly low values. That is two data sources, a disagreement, and its explanation.

whyWrong.A: No hypothesis is proposed and no evidence is weighed for and against one; the text reports a data conflict and its resolution.
whyWrong.B: Costs are never mentioned for either method.
whyWrong.D: The fault lay in the processing software rather than the instrument, and no replacement is proposed.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences explain how ring patterns are matched against a master sequence to fix a felling year. The last sentence adds the catch: the method works only where a master sequence already exists for that species and region, which is why it dominates in the American Southwest and has barely touched the humid tropics. The text describes a method and states what limits it.

whyWrong.B: Radiocarbon dating is never mentioned, so no comparison of accuracy is made.
whyWrong.C: The tropics come up as a place where master sequences are lacking; the text does not claim tropical trees lack visible rings.
whyWrong.D: No history of the method's discovery is given.

whyCorrect: The text pairs a ninth-century date for the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes with the reason scholars once resisted it: they assumed workmanship that fine required contact with Portuguese traders, who arrived centuries later. Radiocarbon dating made that assumption untenable, so the main idea is that the bronzes predate the outside contact the assumption depended on.

whyWrong.A: Independent invention across several parts of Africa is a broader claim than the text makes; only Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Benin are mentioned, and no invention claim is made.
whyWrong.B: The text says early scholars were struck by the fineness of the Igbo-Ukwu work but never ranks it against Ife or Benin.
whyWrong.C: This is the discredited assumption, which the radiocarbon dates overturn.

whyCorrect: The text holds two things together: Domesday is the most complete administrative record surviving from eleventh-century Europe, and it leaves out London, Winchester and most of the north while counting households rather than people. The last sentence names the consequence — historians use it constantly and qualify it constantly. The main idea must keep both halves.

whyWrong.A: London is named as an omission from the survey, not as its purpose.
whyWrong.B: The text says the opposite: it counts households rather than individual people.
whyWrong.D: "Too incomplete to be of much use" contradicts "historians use it constantly" and drops the praise entirely.
