whyCorrect: The archaeologist has to rule out incoming people as the reason the style spread. Ancient DNA showing no change in ancestry across that century means the population stayed the same while the pottery changed, which leaves transmission of the style between existing communities as the explanation.

whyWrong.B: Full coverage of the valley shows how far the style travelled, not whether pots or people did the travelling.
whyWrong.C: Local clay shows the pots were made where they were found, which is compatible with newcomers settling and potting locally.
whyWrong.D: Durability might explain why people wanted the style but says nothing about whether a new population brought it.

whyCorrect: Two changes were made in the same season, so the agronomist needs evidence separating them. Neighbouring farms that adopted the daily irrigation schedule but sowed no cover crops and saw no gain isolate irrigation as ineffective, which leaves the cover crops as the cause of the eighteen percent rise.

whyWrong.A: A further gain the next season is consistent with either change persisting, so it distinguishes nothing.
whyWrong.B: Average rainfall rules out an unusually wet year but says nothing about which of the farmer's two changes mattered.
whyWrong.D: That cover crops build soil organic matter gives a plausible mechanism, but the rival explanation on this farm is irrigation, and this leaves it untouched.

tips: When two changes happen at once, look for the finding that holds one constant and varies the other.

whyCorrect: The simpler explanation says sleep helps only by preventing new input from interfering. Participants kept awake in a dark, silent room get that same freedom from interference without sleeping, so if they still recall less than sleepers, something about sleep itself is doing the work — which is the researcher's active-consolidation proposal.

whyWrong.B: More sleep producing more recall is exactly what the interference account predicts too, since longer sleep also means longer without new input.
whyWrong.C: Learning a second list before sleeping introduces interference and so supports the rival explanation.
whyWrong.D: Reports of dreaming about the material are suggestive but do not show that the dreaming improved recall, and dream reports are not a measure of consolidation.

whyCorrect: Evening ridership on this network rises every autumn anyway, by an average of nine percent from October to December over the previous three years. The observed rise was twelve percent, so most of it is the normal seasonal pattern and only about three points are left for the free fares to explain. Reading the whole twelve percent as the effect of the fare change therefore claims too much for it.

whyWrong.A: The earlier years are precisely what makes the comparison possible; the passage supplies them as the baseline.
whyWrong.B: Riders leaving cycling are part of the seasonal baseline the text describes, and nothing suggests the figure understates them.
whyWrong.D: Twelve percent exceeds the nine percent baseline, so some effect is left over — the text supports a smaller effect, not none.

commonMistakes: When a passage supplies a baseline, the answer is almost always about the difference from it, not the raw number.

whyCorrect: The key sentence is that in the dried state metabolism has stopped altogether — the animal is not living slowly, it is not living at all. Time spent in that state therefore does not count as time lived, so a tardigrade revived after decades of storage tells you nothing about how long the species can live.

whyWrong.B: The passage has already explained the sugar's role: it vitrifies and holds structures in place. The revival records are not what is limited here.
whyWrong.C: Rehydration speed is never discussed, and nothing in the text about stopped metabolism bears on it.
whyWrong.D: Other invertebrates lie outside the passage entirely, and revival records for tardigrades would not be the evidence for them anyway.

whyCorrect: "The admiral who commanded seven voyages across the Indian Ocean" is an appositive naming Zheng He, and the comma after "Zheng He" opens it. A non-essential phrase inside a sentence needs the matching mark at its end, so a comma has to close it before the verb "sailed."

whyWrong.A: Leaving the appositive unclosed runs it straight into the main verb, so the reader never sees where the interruption ends.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and "sailed with fleets larger than any Europe would launch" has no subject.
whyWrong.D: A colon would cut the subject off from its verb and introduces nothing that needs introducing.

whyCorrect: "Three ingredients give the stew its colour" is a complete sentence, and what follows names those three ingredients. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces a list.

whyWrong.A: "But" signals a contrast, and the list names the very ingredients the first clause promised, so there is nothing to oppose.
whyWrong.B: "And" makes the saffron a fourth thing added to the three ingredients rather than one of them, which contradicts the count.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon needs a complete sentence after it, and "saffron, smoked paprika and the fat rendered out of the sausage" is a list of nouns.

whyCorrect: "Whenever the river drops below its summer minimum" is a dependent clause, and it comes first, so a comma joins it to the main clause that follows.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the "Whenever" clause is not independent.
whyWrong.C: A colon also requires a complete clause in front of it.
whyWrong.D: Adding "that" leaves the sentence with no main clause at all — nothing ever gets asserted.

whyCorrect: "Though" makes the first clause dependent, so it cannot be joined by anything that requires two complete sentences. A leading dependent clause takes a comma before the main clause.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon demands an independent clause on both sides, and "Though the score survives only in a copyist's hand" is not one.
whyWrong.B: A colon also requires a complete independent clause before it.
whyWrong.C: "Though" already signals the contrast, and adding "and" leaves the dependent clause with nothing to attach to.

whyCorrect: The three items in the list must take the same form, and the first two are noun phrases built the same way: "the digitisation of the archive" and "the training of local staff." The third has to match, so it is "the construction of a public reading room."

whyWrong.A: "Construct" is a bare verb and cannot serve as the third item in a list of noun phrases.
whyWrong.B: An infinitive breaks the pattern set by the two noun phrases before it.
whyWrong.D: "Constructing" is a gerund, and while it is a noun form, it does not match the "the …" noun phrases used for the other two items.

whyCorrect: "By the time the tide turned" fixes a moment in the past, and the carrying was finished before that moment. An action completed before a stated past time takes the past perfect: "had carried."

whyWrong.B: "Will carry" is future and cannot describe something already done by a past afternoon.
whyWrong.C: "Carry" is present tense and clashes with the past-tense frame the sentence sets up.
whyWrong.D: "Carries" is present tense and singular, disagreeing with the plural sense required and with the past setting.

whyCorrect: With "neither … nor," the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. Here that is "the boiler," which is singular, and the renovation is finished, so the verb is the singular past "was."

whyWrong.A: "Have been" is plural, agreeing with "pipes" rather than the nearer subject "boiler."
whyWrong.B: "Are" is plural and present tense, wrong on both counts.
whyWrong.C: "Were" has the right tense but is plural, so it agrees with the wrong half of the pair.

tips: For "neither … nor" and "either … or," match the verb to whichever subject sits nearer to it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the problem — the dye fades within one season of daylight — and the second gives what museums do about it: dim light and frequent rotation out of the galleries. That is a cause and the practice that follows from it.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" would mark the museums' behaviour as defying the first sentence, but low light is exactly what fading calls for.
whyWrong.B: Nothing is being contrasted; only one dye and one practice appear.
whyWrong.C: "In other words" restates the first sentence, and the second reports a different fact, namely what museums do.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports a reputation for delicacy; the second says a starter neglected for a year can be revived in a week. The second corrects the impression left by the first, and "In fact" is the transition that introduces a reality against a supposed one.

whyWrong.B: "Similarly" adds a parallel point, but the second sentence pushes against the first rather than agreeing with it.
whyWrong.C: A starter surviving a year of neglect is a counterexample to delicacy, not an example of it.
whyWrong.D: "Consequently" makes the resilience a result of the reputation, which is not a causal relationship at all.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general strategy — plants recruiting animals to fight for them — and the second gives one case: acacias housing stinging ants in hollow thorns and paying them in sugar to drive off browsers. Moving from a general claim to a case of it calls for an illustration transition.

whyWrong.A: "Meanwhile" marks something happening at the same time elsewhere, but the acacia is an instance of the claim, not a parallel event.
whyWrong.C: "However" signals contrast, and the acacia confirms rather than opposes the general claim.
whyWrong.D: "Therefore" would make the acacia's arrangement a consequence of the general statement, but a general claim does not cause a particular case.

whyCorrect: The question asks why the hull survived, so the answer must run the mechanism: waterlogged oak splits as it dries, the spray replaced that water with wax cell by cell, and so the timber had nothing left to lose when it dried. Only this choice puts the treatment and the outcome together.

whyWrong.B: This states the danger without saying what prevented it.
whyWrong.C: The sinking and raising dates are background and explain nothing about the timber.
whyWrong.D: The treatment is named but not what it did inside the wood or why that saved the hull.

whyCorrect: The task asks for a specific case of the vault doing its job. The notes contain exactly one: when the seed bank near Aleppo became unreachable in 2015, researchers withdrew the duplicates held at Svalbard. That shows the backup being used for its intended purpose.

whyWrong.A: The vault's location and construction describe how it protects seeds, not an occasion when it was needed.
whyWrong.B: The ownership rule is a general policy rather than a case of the vault being drawn on.
whyWrong.C: This states the vault's general function, which is what the specific case is supposed to illustrate.

whyCorrect: To show that an achievement was short-lived you need both the achievement and its brevity. This choice gives the achievement — ten days cut to minutes — then the failure within three weeks and the eight-year gap before a durable cable worked.

whyWrong.B: This states the achievement alone, which makes the opposite impression.
whyWrong.C: The 1866 date implies a gap but never says what happened in 1858 or that it failed.
whyWrong.D: A completion date on its own says nothing about how long the cable lasted.

whyCorrect: The colon supplies the standard the timing must meet: an error of a few nanoseconds ruins the image. A tolerance that tight demands timing that is extremely strict, and "exacting" is the word for a requirement that allows almost no error.

whyWrong.B: Flexible timing tolerates variation, which is precisely what a few-nanosecond error budget forbids.
whyWrong.C: "Occasional" describes how often something happens, not how precise it is, and intermittent timing would be worse still.
whyWrong.D: "Approximate" is the opposite of what the colon requires — approximation at the nanosecond scale is the failure being described.

whyCorrect: The assumption named at the end is that drivers fill whatever road space exists. Narrowing the avenue should then have crowded it, but traffic fell instead — "Instead" flags the reversal. The blank describes what that result does to the assumption, which is overturn it.

whyWrong.A: A result cannot predict an assumption; prediction runs the other way, and the assumption predicted the opposite outcome.
whyWrong.B: "Confirmed" is backwards: the traffic fell, which is what the assumption said would not happen.
whyWrong.D: "Measured" would make the result a quantity attached to the assumption, but the sentence is about the assumption being wrong.

whyCorrect: The second sentence sets the test of success: the cut works when the absorbed viewer never registers that it happened. A technique designed to go unnoticed is one built to be invisible.

whyWrong.A: "Expressive" would mean the cut draws attention to itself as a statement, the opposite of going unnoticed.
whyWrong.B: Continuity cuts are certainly deliberate, but that describes the editor's intention rather than the effect on the viewer that the second sentence measures.
whyWrong.D: "Abrupt" describes a cut the viewer feels, which is exactly the failure the second sentence rules out.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts amber with mudstone, where the same structure survives only as a stain. In amber the wing keeps detail down to individual hairs on its trailing edge, so the blank has to mean whole and undamaged.

whyWrong.A: "Altered" says the membrane changed, which contradicts the surviving hair-level detail and destroys the contrast with the stain.
whyWrong.B: Nothing suggests resin makes a specimen larger; the point is fidelity, not size.
whyWrong.C: Compression is what happens to fossils in rock, so this describes the mudstone side of the contrast rather than the amber side.

whyCorrect: The second half of the sentence gives the outcome: they surrender more time in the closing stretch than the fast start ever won them. So the blank must describe them losing pace over the final third.

whyWrong.A: Accelerating would mean going faster, which cannot cost them time.
whyWrong.C: "Recover" implies they get the pace back, contradicting the net loss of time described.
whyWrong.D: "Persist" says they keep going at the same rate, which again leaves the surrendered time unexplained.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence lays down the rule — a desert is defined by precipitation, not heat. The middle sentence gives the case that shows it, Antarctica's interior qualifying as the largest desert on earth, and the last sentence puts the rule again in other words. So it states the principle the rest of the text illustrates and restates.

whyWrong.A: No geographers are quoted and no disagreement is described; the text presents a single settled criterion.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is conceded — the text agrees with the underlined sentence throughout and never disputes it.
whyWrong.D: It gives the definition rather than an example; Antarctica is the example, and it comes afterwards.

whyCorrect: The text sets two things side by side: the Babylonian wedge, which only marked an empty column, and Brahmagupta's rules, which treat zero as a quantity you can add, subtract and multiply. The last two sentences make the point explicit — the symbol was old, its standing as a number was not. The purpose is to separate the earlier use from the later, weightier one.

whyWrong.B: Babylonian mathematics is described, not defended; no claim about neglect by historians appears.
whyWrong.C: The rules are mentioned as a category of what Brahmagupta did, but none is actually set out.
whyWrong.D: No route of transmission is traced; the text does not claim India took the symbol from Babylon.

whyCorrect: The text builds one line of argument: fog arrives most mornings in a place that almost never sees rain, the beetles climb the dunes and tilt to catch it, droplets run down grooves to the mouth, and this supplies nearly all their water. The main idea is that the beetles drink fog rather than rain.

whyWrong.A: No inland comparison is made; the fog is described only where the beetles are.
whyWrong.C: Other deserts at similar latitudes never appear in the text.
whyWrong.D: "Only animals capable of surviving" is far stronger than anything stated; the text describes one adaptation, not an exclusive one.

whyCorrect: The transplant result is stated directly: colonies given the unusual algal strain survive temperatures that bleach untreated colonies on the same reef. Same reef and same coral species means the coral is held constant and only the algae differ, so the tolerance is shown to lie with the algae.

whyWrong.A: The experiments compared corals hosting different algae; nothing was tested about algae living outside coral tissue.
whyWrong.C: No claim about a distinct coral species is made, and the comparison within a single reef would not establish one.
whyWrong.D: Recovery after cooling is never discussed; the experiments concern resistance to bleaching, not repair afterwards.

whyCorrect: The two explanations point at different variables: predators absent versus island small. The finding that decides between them holds one variable across a wide range while the other stays fixed. Flightless rails occurring on islands of widely varying size, but only where mammalian predators were absent, shows size does not track flightlessness and predator absence does.

whyWrong.A: Smaller flight muscles describe what flightlessness consists of, not why it evolved, and both accounts predict it.
whyWrong.B: More frequent storms around remote islands supports the rival account, since being blown out to sea is its mechanism.
whyWrong.C: When the rails arrived dates the colonisations without bearing on either cause.

tips: When two explanations compete, look for the finding in which one candidate cause varies and the outcome does not follow it.

whyCorrect: The archaeologist's claim is about purpose: ceremony rather than haulage. A road that holds its width and bearing straight over ridges a loaded traveller would have walked around is built against the interests of anyone carrying goods, since the grade costs effort for nothing. Sacrificing practicality to keep the line straight is what a processional route would do.

whyWrong.A: Construction in stages tells you how long the road took to build, not what it was used for.
whyWrong.C: Its exceptional width is already given in the passage and is consistent with heavy transport as much as with ceremony.
whyWrong.D: Pottery carried to the shrine shows goods did move along the route, which if anything supports the everyday-transport reading.

whyCorrect: Both explanations cover the same fifteen years, so the useful evidence separates them geographically. The waters immediately outside the reserve had the same warm springs but no fishing ban, and cod there did not recover — warm springs alone therefore do not produce recovery, which leaves the ban as the difference that mattered.

whyWrong.A: Greater average length inside the reserve is expected under either account once fish are left alone or spawning improves, and length is not the recovery being explained.
whyWrong.B: Warm springs starting in the reserve's first year makes the two causes coincide more exactly, which makes them harder to tell apart, not easier.
whyWrong.C: More fishing effort outside the reserve is a fact about the fleet and does not show what caused the increase inside.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up a gap between what works and what feels as though it works: spaced sessions produce better recall a month later, while the single-sitting students feel more confident because massed material is fluent while still fresh. A student choosing by that feeling is steered toward the single sitting, which is the method with the weaker month-later result.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the two methods differ noticeably in felt confidence, so a student judging by feel would perceive a difference — just the wrong one.
whyWrong.C: Total study time is held equal in the comparison, so neither method costs more time.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the finding; choosing by feel leads to the method that leaves less in memory.

commonMistakes: When a passage separates felt effectiveness from measured effectiveness, the completion almost always says the feeling misleads.

whyCorrect: Three points define a scale here. Teosinte carries a handful of kernels in one row; the market cob carries several hundred in a dozen or more rows; the 5,000-year-old cobs sit between them at eight rows of small kernels. Being well past the wild ancestor and well short of the modern cob is what those numbers say.

whyWrong.A: Eight rows is far beyond teosinte's single row, so substantial change had already occurred, which is evidence of cultivation rather than against it.
whyWrong.C: Five centimetres with eight rows is nothing like a modern cob of several hundred kernels in a dozen or more rows.
whyWrong.D: The text describes cobs from one site but says nothing about where else maize was or was not grown.

whyCorrect: "The tin contains everything needed for a first repair" is a complete sentence, and what follows spells out what "everything" consists of. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces such a list.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, but "a spool of solder, a length of shrink tubing and a spare fuse" is a list of noun phrases.
whyWrong.C: "And" adds the solder as one more thing alongside "everything needed," instead of presenting it as part of that everything.
whyWrong.D: "Which is" is singular while three items follow, and the relative clause is left unpunctuated as though it were essential to identifying the repair.

whyCorrect: "The vaccination team reached the last village in the district in March" and "the outbreak was declared over in July" both stand alone as sentences, and no conjunction is offered. Two independent clauses in that position require a semicolon.

whyWrong.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: A colon promises that what follows explains or specifies the first clause, but a later declaration is a separate event in the sequence.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into a run-on.

whyCorrect: Each half is a full sentence: the balloon rose for forty minutes, and then it began to sink. "Then" is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot join them — a semicolon is needed.

whyWrong.A: Without punctuation the clauses run together as a fused sentence.
whyWrong.C: A comma before the adverb "then" still leaves two independent clauses spliced by a comma.
whyWrong.D: A colon signals explanation or specification, but the sinking is the next event rather than an unpacking of the ascent.

whyCorrect: "A stepwell cut into the ground in Gujarat in the eleventh century" renames Rani ki Vav and is opened by the comma after the name. A non-essential appositive dropped between subject and verb needs a comma at both ends, so one has to close it before "descends."

whyWrong.A: With no closing comma the appositive runs into the verb and the sentence never marks where the interruption ends.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, and "descends seven storeys and carries more than five hundred sculpted figures" has no subject.
whyWrong.D: A colon separates the subject from its verb and introduces nothing.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The number," which is singular; "of applicants to the conservation course" is a prepositional phrase and cannot contain the subject. The sentence also needs the auxiliary that goes with "risen," so the answer is "has risen."

whyWrong.A: "Were" is plural and cannot combine with the participle "risen" to form the perfect.
whyWrong.B: "Have" is the plural auxiliary, agreeing with "applicants" instead of with "number."
whyWrong.D: "Are" is plural and, like "were," cannot pair with "risen."

commonMistakes: "The number of X" is singular; "a number of X" is plural. The article decides it.

whyCorrect: The sentence is inverted: it opens with the prepositional phrase "Among the papers found at the back of the architect's desk," and the real subject comes after the verb. That subject is "a letter," which is singular, so the verb is "was."

whyWrong.A: "Were" agrees with "papers," but that noun sits inside the opening prepositional phrase and cannot be the subject.
whyWrong.C: "Have been" is plural and also shifts into the present perfect for no reason.
whyWrong.D: "Are" is plural and present tense, disagreeing with the singular subject and with the past setting.

tips: When a sentence starts with a preposition and no subject appears before the verb, find the subject after the verb.

whyCorrect: "Walking the shoreline at first light" is a participial modifier, and the noun immediately after the comma is what it describes. Only a person can walk a shoreline, so the main clause has to open with the person doing the walking. "The collector found a line of amber" supplies that subject.

whyWrong.A: "There" is a placeholder with no one to attach the modifier to, leaving the participle dangling.
whyWrong.B: This makes the tide the thing walking the shoreline at first light.
whyWrong.C: With "a line of amber" as the subject, the sentence says the amber was walking the shoreline.

commonMistakes: An opening -ing phrase attaches to whatever noun comes right after the comma, however far from the intended meaning that is.

whyCorrect: The first sentence is a fifty-year record of reliable service, a clear positive. The second raises a real operational cost: fresh water consumed fast enough to limit time at sea. A drawback set against an established strength needs a concessive transition.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" adds a similar point, and heavy water use is not similar to reliability.
whyWrong.B: "In summary" would close a discussion, but the second sentence introduces new information.
whyWrong.D: "Therefore" would make the water consumption a consequence of launching aircraft reliably, which reverses the relationship — the consumption is a cost of the mechanism, not a result of its reliability.

whyCorrect: The second sentence adds no new fact. That every map distorts something, and that the cartographer only chooses what to distort, is the same content as "no projection can preserve area and shape at once" put in plainer terms. A restatement transition is what marks that.

whyWrong.A: No particular map or projection is named, so this is not an example.
whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" signals a contrast, but the second sentence agrees with the first completely.
whyWrong.C: "Earlier" marks time sequence, and neither sentence describes an event.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the evidence — tin from Cornwall and copper from the eastern Alps in one object — and the second draws what follows from it: the workshop was supplied by trade running across the continent. That is an inference transition.

whyWrong.A: "Meanwhile" marks two things happening at once, not evidence and conclusion.
whyWrong.B: "Admittedly" concedes a point that works against the writer, and this conclusion is the writer's own.
whyWrong.D: "Conversely" introduces an opposite case, but the second sentence follows from the first rather than opposing it.

whyCorrect: The task names one feature serving two purposes, so the sentence must name the feature and both things it does. This choice identifies the narrow slit and then gives both effects: it blocks glare off the snow and, like a pinhole, sharpens distant objects.

whyWrong.A: This names the feature but neither of its purposes.
whyWrong.B: This gives one effect and never ties it to the goggles' slit.
whyWrong.C: The materials are a different fact about the goggles and serve neither purpose named in the task.

whyCorrect: "Unusually informative" needs both what the Ebla tablets preserve and what makes that unusual. This choice gives the fire that baked and hardened the clay, the shelf order preserved with it, and the contrast with the scattered, unbaked fragments that make up most cuneiform archives — order in an archive is itself evidence.

whyWrong.A: A count of tablets and a discovery date say nothing about what makes the archive exceptional.
whyWrong.B: The baking is half the story, but with no mention of the preserved order or of how other archives survive, nothing marks it as unusual.
whyWrong.D: This describes other archives only, leaving Ebla out of the sentence entirely.
